protections: P1 (address): an object-supplied Vault address must pass an operator allowlist and an SSRF guard before it becomes the address of the webhook's own Vault client, which carries a ServiceAccount token the webhook obtained for the object-named SA; an operator-configured vault_addr is trusted and must not be forced through that policy. One guard (common.ValidateObjectAddr, pkg/common/addr.go:42) closes the annotation case and the operator-default case is the coupled exemption.

P2 (TLS skip): an object-supplied vault-skip-verify must not disable certificate verification on the webhook's own Vault connection unless the operator opted in; otherwise the operator's vault_skip_verify applies. Separate control, separate helper (common.ResolveObjectSkipVerify, pkg/common/policy.go:44), separate operator key.

P3 (sibling, same rule, different transport): an object-supplied registry-skip-verify must not disable verification on the webhook's outbound image-registry transport without operator opt-in; the operator key registry_skip_verify already exists (pkg/webhook/config.go:502). This protection is not mentioned by the advisory but is the same rule applied to the only other outbound connection the webhook owns.

traps.reason_to_dismiss: Just call the guard unconditionally in newVaultClient: every address that reaches it is 'object-supplied' from the solver's point of view, and a default-deny allowlist is the safest posture.
The token is minted for an SA in the object's own namespace and is never returned to the requester, so placing the address check anywhere before the login at webhook.go:310 still prevents the SSRF.

vault-skip-verify is a documented user-facing annotation (the chart README recommends it verbatim), so honouring it is the feature, not the bug; and no operator opt-in key exists in the tree to honour it with.

registry-skip-verify is a separate documented feature for private registries with self-signed certificates (different annotation, different outbound connection); the advisory names the Vault address, not the registry transport, so it needs no change.

The webhook never dials that address: the mutated workload does, with the tenant's own ServiceAccount, and the tenant can set VAULT_ADDR in its own pod anyway. The annotation is the documented purpose of the feature, and the e2e fixtures rely on a non-default value.

The Secret is read from the webhook's own namespace (webhook.go:214-215), so a tenant cannot plant the CA; only an existing operator-created Secret can be named, and the pool replaces system roots only for the operator-named CA.

Once the address is operator-approved these are documented annotations, and the auth exchange still happens against the operator's Vault, which authorises the role; Vault, not the webhook, is the policy decision point for path and auth method.
The SA is looked up and minted in the object's own namespace (webhook.go:260, 285), so a tenant can only name SAs it shares a namespace with, and the minted token is not returned to the requester.

masking: The pinned commit already contains the policy library and its full behavioural test table with no production caller (pkg/common/addr.go:42, pkg/common/policy.go:44; callers exist only in pkg/common/addr_test.go:172 and pkg/common/policy_test.go:56), so the shape questions ('which inputs must be refused') are pre-answered in-tree and only the wiring decision remains; the dead helpers mask the difficulty of M8-style traps.

The coupled T2 only becomes visible after T1 is fixed: an unconditional guard in newVaultClient breaks pkg/webhook/webhook_test.go:118-122 (httptest address http://127.0.0.1:PORT), which is a default-mode unit test, so the over-broad fix is detected by the repository's own suite rather than by a hidden test.

Fixing P1 at the loader instead of the client factory makes the pod path reject a legitimate annotation, which is the failure mode the e2e fixtures encode (e2e/test/deployment.yaml:15, e2e/test/configmap.yaml:6, e2e/test/secret.yaml:6); that constraint is only observable once someone tries the loader.

conflicts.what: Validating the annotation in the only producer, parseVaultConfig (pkg/webhook/config.go:107-111), closes T1 for all four routes at once but also rewrites the value handed to the mutated workload (pkg/webhook/pod.go:90) and to the operator-default path; if the check is applied unconditionally it rejects the operator default https://vault:8200 (pkg/webhook/config.go:474) and the in-repo client test that uses an httptest loopback address (pkg/webhook/webhook_test.go:118-122). The correct split needs a provenance flag on VaultConfig so only the annotation-derived address is vetted.

SkipVerify is a single field with two consumers: the webhook's own TLS (pkg/webhook/webhook.go:206) and the env it writes into every mutated container (pkg/webhook/pod.go:94, 334). Gating the field in parseVaultConfig (the only producer) necessarily changes container behaviour that the chart README tells users to rely on (deploy/charts/vault-secrets-webhook/README.md:18); gating it only at webhook.go:206 leaves the container value object-controlled. Satisfying both needs the gated and propagated values to be separated.

Any identity-side fix for the object-named SA has to work for /secrets and /configmaps, which have no service account of their own, and cannot compare against a pod SA because VaultConfig carries no such field (pkg/webhook/config.go:88); a naive binding check breaks pkg/webhook/webhook_test.go:50-57, which passes VaultConfig with only VaultServiceAccount set.

fairness_risks: The operator knobs the fix needs (an address allowlist, a private-address opt-in, an object-skip-verify opt-in) do not exist anywhere in the pinned tree: no such viper key, chart value, env name or doc line is present, and only the test-local names test_allow_object_skip_verify / test_skip_verify appear (pkg/common/policy_test.go:33-34). If hidden tests set the real key names, they must be stated in the task report or the accepted-address and honoured-opt-in cases are unguessable.

The guard is default-deny on an empty allowlist (pkg/common/addr_test.go:48-53), so a rule 'object address must be allowlisted' contradicts the repository's own e2e fixtures, which set non-default addresses with no allowlist configured (e2e/test/deployment.yaml:15, e2e/test/configmap.yaml:6, e2e/test/secret.yaml:6). Grading 'annotation still works' and 'annotation rejected' together is only possible if the test configures the allowlist.

The rule 'every address passed to newVaultClient is checked' contradicts pkg/webhook/webhook_test.go:118-122 (httptest loopback) and pkg/webhook/configmap_test.go:33,60 (http://localhost:8200); the must-keep-working behaviour is enforced by the repo itself, so the hidden tests must not demand an unconditional check.

Grading the /pods env propagation (T5) as a missing protection would contradict the documented purpose of the annotation (deploy/charts/vault-secrets-webhook/README.md:14-18, e2e/test/deployment-template.yaml:56) and provide no security benefit, since the tenant writes its own pod env anyway (pkg/webhook/pod.go:327-335).
The refusal shapes are already fully specified by an in-tree test table (pkg/common/addr_test.go:23-180), so any hidden test that only re-asserts those shapes passes without any production change.

parseVaultConfig and newVaultClient are unexported and no test calls the annotation loader (no test references parseVaultConfig), so hidden tests must live in package webhook or drive VaultSecretsMutator; a harness that drives the HTTP handlers would need a fake clientset for the token mint and the TLS-Secret read.

design.why: Three independent groups, each with a different dismissal and a different fix site, all on the webhook's own credential-bearing outbound connections so no documented tenant use is broken. G1 (T1+T2+T6): the address policy must be enforced in newVaultClient with an explicit provenance flag and before the ServiceAccount token mint (pkg/webhook/webhook.go:204, 285-296) - the naive unconditional call is the MiMo failure mode and is caught by the repo's own test (pkg/webhook/webhook_test.go:118-122). G2 (T3): a second, separate control with its own helper and its own operator opt-in, so a solver who only fixes the address still leaves TLS verification object-controlled (pkg/webhook/config.go:147-151 -> pkg/webhook/webhook.go:206). G3 (T4): the same rule on the webhook's only other outbound transport, reachable from the same annotation loader, with a ready-made operator default (pkg/webhook/config.go:502) and a strong 'different documented feature' dismissal - the DeepSeek failure mode. This beats designs built on T5 (documented pod behaviour, no security gain, breaks e2e fixtures), T7 (the CA is read from the webhook's own namespace, so there is no tenant-controlled trust material) and T9 (no upstream change, and no definable policy for objects that have no SA), and it beats a single-site design because loader placement and factory placement conflict: one trap rewards each, which is exactly the judgement the stacked task should measure.
